analysis.one_liner: Delays EPA's review of the ozone smog standard by three years and stretches future reviews to every ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill to postpone EPA's ozone standard review never came up for a vote; it died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee after a single hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Clean Air Act, EPA must review the national limit on ground-level ozone — the main ingredient in smog — every five years, and can move faster if the science warrants. This bill would stretch that cycle to ten years and, for ozone specifically, bar EPA from reviewing or tightening the standard before a set deadline, even if its own science advisers recommend it. The practical effect would be to keep the existing ozone limit in place years longer, delaying any new cleanup requirements for smog-forming pollution.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that emit ozone-forming pollution — fossil-fuel producers, manufacturers, power plants, and vehicle fleets — would gain the most, because a stricter ozone standard eventually forces them to install controls or change operations. States and localities would also avoid the work of writing new compliance plans. Health groups and public-health researchers would lose the chance to have the standard updated on the normal five-year cycle.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Smog-emitting industries and their state regulators

how_it_helps.text: The bill changes the Clean Air Act review cycle for national air quality standards from every five years to every ten years [S2][S3].

It specifically bars EPA from reviewing or revising the ozone standard before a fixed date and eliminates EPA's existing authority to review ozone standards earlier or more often than the regular cycle [S2][S3].
It also delays the review by EPA's independent science advisory committee of the ozone standard until the same fixed date [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who breathe the air. Ground-level ozone is linked to asthma attacks, reduced lung function, and other respiratory harm, so delaying a possible tightening of the standard means those health costs continue longer. Communities near highways, industrial facilities, and oil and gas operations bear the largest share.

drawbacks.text: Supporters' rationale was that EPA had just completed an ozone review and was revisiting a recently updated standard ahead of the normal five-year cycle, creating regulatory uncertainty for states and businesses that had just begun compliance planning [S2][S3].

Even a supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: stretching the review cycle to ten years means public-health protections lag behind current science for longer, and the bill removed EPA's flexibility to act early when the science advisory committee recommends it [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real relief from compliance uncertainty for regulated industries and states, at the cost of slower updates to a health standard that protects people from smog. Because the changes were permanent (a ten-year cycle) and ozone-specific (locking in a deadline regardless of new science), the public-health cost would have compounded over time rather than been a one-time delay.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate environment committee, got one hearing in June 2015, and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 3, 2015 by Sen. Jeff Flake with ten original Republican co-introducers, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S3][S5].
Thirteen Republican senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee held a hearing on the bill on June 3, 2015 (printed as S.Hrg. 114-47) but never voted to report it out [S5].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 114th Congress, so the bill never received a floor vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead in the narrow sense that the delay was never enacted, leaving EPA's authority to review and tighten the ozone standard intact on the existing five-year cycle. Industries that emit smog-forming pollution did not get the extended deadline the bill would have provided, though the hearing record shows the issue stayed on the agenda for them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday people; EPA's ozone review authority stayed intact

for.name: Sen. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited ten original co-introducers.

for.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee majority
for.what_they_did: Gave the bill a hearing in June 2015, its only committee action.

sides.party_line_note: All fourteen Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on.

industries.note: Fossil-fuel operations are a major source of the emissions that create ground-level ozone, and a stricter standard would require added controls and permits. The bill would have pushed any tightening off for years, keeping their compliance costs down at the expense of air quality.

Factories and power plants that emit ozone-forming pollution would face new control requirements if the standard were tightened; the bill would defer that cost indefinitely. The savings come from leaving the existing smog limit in place longer.

A delay would spare states the expense of drafting new air-quality compliance plans, but many states also bear the health costs of smog within their borders. The relief is administrative; the underlying pollution burden is unchanged.
